- Market structure from text and baskets. @netzer2012 convert online user-generated content
  into perceptual maps of competing car models and drugs, and validate them against sales and
  survey data. @lee2011automated elicit attributes and relative brand positions from reviews.
  @gabel2019map derive latent product attributes from co-occurrence in shopping baskets with a
  neural language model, which recovers complementarity across categories as well as
  substitution within them. These are the product-level counterparts of the firm-level text and
  graph methods discussed above, built a decade earlier and validated against demand.

On the managerial side, @clark1999managerial studied how managers actually identify competitors
and proposed a cognitive framework for it. @bergen2002competitor and @peteraf2003scanning
developed a framework that identifies competitors by market commonality and by resource
equivalence, so that potential and indirect competitors, which substitute on the supply side,
enter the analysis. @chen1996competitor's integration of competitor analysis and interfirm
rivalry rests on the same two dimensions. For industry assignment, the implication is that a
complete scheme would combine a demand-side notion (who substitutes for whom) with a
supply-side one (who could enter), and neither SIC nor annual-report text measures the first
directly.

For a marketing researcher, the payoff is a reframing. What the strategy literature calls the
industry effect is, in marketing's terms, the effect of the competitive market structure that a
firm faces. Marketing has better tools for measuring that structure than the classification
schemes the strategy literature uses. It also has the most to lose from bad assignment, because
the marketing-mix and marketing–finance literatures routinely use industry as a control or a
benchmark: industry-adjusted Tobin's *q*, industry-year means of advertising intensity, and
industry-level frontiers for capability, as in @sec-capability.

## What to Do Differently {#sec-ie-practice}

The argument of this chapter turns into a short set of habits for empirical work.

1. *Report the assignment as a modelling choice.* Name the scheme, the level, the source
   database, and whether codes are header or historical [@kahle1996industry]. When the result
   depends on industry, through a fixed effect, an industry-adjusted variable, or a peer
   benchmark, re-estimate it under at least one scheme built on a different basis: a vendor code
   (GICS), a text-based scheme (TNIC), or a peer-based one.
2. *Match schemes on granularity.* Compare schemes with the same number of groups, and report
   group-size distributions. As @vanneste2017howmuch showed for sums of squares, sample
   dimensions alone can move an estimate, and a comparison of SIC2 with a 400-group text
   clustering confounds the basis of similarity with the fineness of the partition.
3. *Benchmark against chance.* Permute industry labels across firms, preserving the number and
   sizes of groups, and report the industry share that random assignment produces, in the spirit
   of @fitza2014ceo. An industry effect is informative only relative to that floor.
4. *Validate on a criterion the scheme was not built from.* A text scheme will always look
   best on text similarity. Comovement of sales growth, returns, or margins, in the tradition of
   @bhojraj2003line, is a fairer test, and so is an outcome-based test such as the one in
   @eshraghi2026industry.
5. *Decide what the industry effect is supposed to be.* A product-market grouping (rivals), a
   value-chain grouping (suppliers and customers), and a perceptual grouping (who analysts and
   investors compare) measure different environments. State which one the theory needs, and
   choose the data accordingly. For marketing questions, demand-side substitution is usually
   the right construct, and marketing's market-structure tools measure it most directly, as
   @sec-ie-marketing describes.
6. *Treat industry as a substantive competitor, not a nuisance.* The fixed effect may absorb the
   variation that most needs explaining, as @sec-marketing-strategy argued. A poor grouping
   leaves part of that variation in the error term, so the problem cuts both ways.

Several questions remain open and would make good dissertation chapters.

- Time-varying assignment. Most decompositions, including the replication here, fix each firm's
  industry. Text and network schemes can be re-estimated every year, which turns industry
  membership into a dynamic variable, and the variance decomposition would then need a model in
  which firms move between levels.
- Overlap and asymmetry. Multiple-membership models [@browne2001mmmc] handle firms in several
  markets. No standard decomposition handles asymmetric competition, in which A's presence
  constrains B more than B's constrains A [@desarbo2006competes].
- Endogenous assignment. Firms choose their markets and write the text from which they are
  classified [@hoberg2016tnic]. If performance drives repositioning, the assignment is a
  function of the outcome, and the decomposition needs a design that breaks that loop, such as
  assignment from lagged text or from third-party data (analysts, customers).
- Which relations define an industry. A heterogeneous graph [@shi2024heterogeneous] can be asked
  which edge types carry the industry effect, through the meta-path weights of an attention
  model [@wang2019han] or by comparing decompositions under graphs that include or exclude each
  layer. This would give an empirical answer to the conceptual question raised in
  @sec-ie-positioning.

## Key Takeaways {#sec-ie-takeaways}

- The share of performance variance attributed to industry is a joint property of the economy
  and of the classification scheme. Misassignment does not add noise; it relabels industry
  variance as firm variance, in proportion to how poorly the scheme's groups capture the
  environments firms actually share (@eq-ie-ltv).
- Four decades of variance decomposition interrogated the estimator, the outcome, the sample, the
  levels, the time window, and the effect-size metric. The meta-analytic consensus (variance
  shares of 0.08 for industry, 0.14 for corporation, 0.36 for business; @vanneste2017howmuch)
  rests almost entirely on SIC codes.
- @eshraghi2026industry show that schemes disagree substantially about which firms belong
  together, that some firms are grouped together consistently and many are not, and that
  schemes grouping more similar firms yield stronger industry effects. Industry has likely been
  underestimated.
- Our replication on a Compustat panel shows the same pattern on public text data (TNIC) and on a
  multiplex network of six inter-firm relations: low agreement with SIC, better comovement at
  matched granularity, and a larger industry share than SIC at the same number of groups, as
  reported in @sec-ie-replication.
- Text describes what firms sell; relations describe what firms do with each other. Heterogeneous
  graphs [@shi2024heterogeneous] combine both, but they mix similarity with complementarity, so
  the researcher must decide which notion of industry the theory requires.
- Marketing's demand-side tools for estimating competitive market structure measure the
  construct that industry effects are supposed to capture more directly than any classification
  scheme does.

## Further Reading {#sec-ie-further}

For the variance decomposition debate, read @rumelt1991industry and @mcgahan1997really as a
pair, then @mcgahan2002variance for the reconciliation, @vanneste2017howmuch for the
meta-analysis, and @wang2023changes for how the answer has changed over time.
@sharapov2021shapley is the best single reference on estimators. For classification, start with
@bhojraj2003line and @hoberg2016tnic, then @kaustia2021common for a peer-based alternative. For
the categorical view, @zuckerman1999categorical and @cattani2017categories. For the marketing
side, @day1979productmarkets, @desarbo2006competes, and @ringel2016asymmetric. The organizing
paper, @eshraghi2026industry, is open access.
